Five databases were searched for randomized controlled trials published from January 2005-12 April 2026. Random-effects pairwise meta-analyses and frequentist network meta-analyses were conducted using standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Risk of bias and confidence in network estimates were assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool and CINeMA, respectively. Thirty-six reports met the eligibility criteria, and 35 reports involving 1694 children contributed to the quantitative synthesis. Non-pharmacological interventions produced a statistically significant moderate overall improvement in cognitive outcomes (standardized mean difference = 0.54, 95% confidence interval 0.36-0.71), with significant benefits for working memory (0.61, 0.09-1.13) and social-emotional cognition (0.47, 0.30-0.65). Social-emotional cognition was the only domain with a sufficiently connected network for comparisons across intervention categories; social-behavioral and technology- and robot-assisted interventions showed the clearest benefits relative to active controls. Evidence networks for attention, working memory, and comprehensive executive function were sparse or disconnected. Confidence was moderate for selected social-emotional cognition comparisons but low or very low for most estimates. Non-pharmacological interventions may improve selected cognitive outcomes in children with autism spectrum disorder, but effects appear domain specific. More adequately powered head-to-head trials using standardized outcomes are needed.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. ValidYN="Y">10.1016/j.jcomdis.2026.106701</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">S0021-9924(26)00085-7</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Developmental stuttering is a multifactorial speech disorder that emerges during early childhood and can persist into adulthood, affecting communication, social participation, and quality of life. Recent research has increasingly focused on the role of executive functions (EFs)-including working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility-in the onset and persistence of stuttering. This scoping review systematically maps the existing literature on EFs in monolingual individuals who stutter across the lifespan, synthesizing findings from 89 studies published between 1993 and 2024. Studies were identified through comprehensive searches of major databases and screened according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The review highlights methodological diversity, participant characteristics, and thematic trends in the assessment of EFs using behavioral tasks and parent-report measures. While findings are often inconsistent, a substantial body of evidence suggests that people who stutter may demonstrate diminished performance in one or more EF domains, particularly working memory and cognitive flexibility. Notably, only a few studies have examined all three core EF components simultaneously, and intervention studies remain limited. The review identifies key gaps in the literature, including the need for studies that could provide a longitudinal and comprehensive insight of all components of EFs within homogeneous populations, as well as further EF-based intervention research in stuttering. These insights underscore the potential of EF-focused approaches to enhance stuttering assessment and treatment.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Inc. ValidYN="Y">10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1865879</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Childhood and adolescence are a critical period for brain development, yet global physical inactivity threatens this neurodevelopmental trajectory. This review synthesizes the past decade of evidence on how physical exercise modulates executive function and emotional brain circuitry in youth. Behaviorally, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise may enhance inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. However, effect sizes are consistently small-to-moderate, and not all cognitive domains show uniform benefits, with working memory effects being smaller and more variable, and high-intensity exercise sometimes impairing performance. Neuroimaging findings reveal enhanced prefrontal-amygdala functional connectivity, strengthening top-down emotion regulation. Mechanistically, acute exercise appears to enhance cognition via transient neurochemical and hemodynamic changes, while chronic exercise may induce longer-lasting neuroplasticity through BDNF-related pathways, although these mechanisms remain largely inferred and peripheral BDNF is an imperfect surrogate for central activity. Cognitively engaging activities yield superior benefits, with the most consistently supported protocols involving approximately 45-min sessions, three times weekly, sustained for 12 weeks or longer. These parameters represent modal characteristics of successful interventions rather than precisely established optimal prescriptions, and substantial heterogeneity across studies precludes highly specific, universally applicable recommendations. Notably, neurodevelopmental populations like ADHD exhibit distinct or amplified responsiveness. Key limitations include methodological heterogeneity, fragmented causal inference, small sample sizes in neuroimaging studies, and limited evidence for clinical populations. Future work must advance precision exercise prescriptions based on individual neural profiles and translational research bridging laboratory findings with real-world educational We evaluated exercise effectiveness on these domains in pre-frail and frail older adults.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">We searched four databases to 8 June 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Meta-analyses utilized the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model. Evidence certainty was assessed using GRADE.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">Included were 37 RCTs (3409 participants). Exercise significantly reduced frailty scores (SMD = -0.95, 95% CI: -1.38 to -0.51, P < 0.001). Physical function improved, including Grip Strength (MD = 1.78 kg, 95% CI: 0.34-3.21, P = 0.020), gait speed (SMD = 1.10, 95% CI: 0.71-1.48, P < 0.001), and SPPB (MD = 1.14 points, 95% CI: 0.53-1.74, P < 0.001). Global cognition (SMD = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.50-0.85, P < 0.001), cognitive flexibility, and working memory improved significantly; executive function and processing speed showed marginal significance. Frail individuals showed larger effect sizes for frailty scores and SPPB than pre-frail individuals. Improvements in Grip Strength, SPPB, and sit-to-stand performance approached or exceeded MCID thresholds, but wide confidence intervals make clinical gains likely rather than confirmed. GRADE certainty ranged from high to very low.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">Exercise may improve frailty status, physical, and cognitive function, particularly for individuals with established frailty. However, substantial heterogeneity limits findings' precision. Multicomponent training appears promising and clinically practical, but current evidence does not establish its superiority over single-modality exercise.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 Elsevier B.V. ValidYN="Y">10.3389/fimmu.2026.1940736</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Endometriosis is an estrogen-dependent inflammatory disorder that often persists or returns even after visible lesions have been removed. The behavior of peritoneal macrophages may help explain this clinical durability. These cells participate in lesion implantation, vascularization, fibrosis, defective immune clearance, and pain, but it is uncertain why disease-supporting phenotypes are maintained. We argue that repeated exposure to the endometriotic niche may leave macrophages with a metabolically conditioned epigenetic memory rather than only a short-lived polarization state. Lactate, succinate, iron, oxysterols, and glutamine-derived metabolites could alter cellular metabolism while also providing substrates, cofactors, or inhibitors for chromatin-modifying enzymes. Histone lactylation and TET/JmjC-regulated methylation states are plausible molecular records of this exposure, although neither has yet been followed from metabolite to persistent mark and macrophage function in human disease. At present, the most direct endometriosis-specific support comes from a TGF-β1/CCL2-induced TET3 program associated with let-7 repression, inflammatory cytokine production, and macrophage survival. Other proposed circuits, including lactate-lactylation coupling and macrophage-stromal exchange of glycolytic signals, remain incomplete. This distinction matters: established findings support parts of the model, but not yet the entire causal chain. A memory state should be experimentally identifiable by its persistence after stimulus withdrawal, transferability, metabolic dependence, and reversibility. If experiments satisfy these criteria, the retained macrophage state would become a plausible non-hormonal target. Methodological quality was assessed using the PEDro scale, and the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system. Meta-analysis was conducted using a three-level random-effects model in R software, and publication bias was examined. Effect sizes were estimated using Hedges' <i>g</i> with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and 95% prediction intervals (PIs) were calculated to determine the expected range of effect sizes in future comparable studies. Funnel plots and Egger's regression test were used to assess publication bias.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">A total of 10 RCTs comprising 623 older adults with MCI from community settings, hospitals, and nursing homes were included. The interventions consisted primarily of multicomponent exercise at moderate intensity, with session durations of 30-90 min, frequencies of 2-5 sessions per week, and intervention periods of 8-48 weeks. Control groups received usual care or health education. Most studies reported no exercise-related adverse events. The mean PEDro score of the included studies was 6.0. The three-level meta-analysis revealed that multicomponent exercise significantly improved global cognitive function (<i>g</i> = 1.063, 95% CI [0.355, 1.771], <i>p</i> = 0.007, 95% PI [-1.141, 3.267]) and executive function (<i>g</i> = 0.372, 95% CI [0.140, 0.604], <i>p</i> = 0.005, 95% PI [0.140, 0.604]) in older adults with MCI. BDNF was assessed in only two studies, with conflicting findings, and its effects remain inconclusive. Exploratory subgroup analyses revealed that none of the moderator variables reached statistical significance: exercise duration [<i>F</i>(1,9) = 0.127, <i>p</i> = 0.730], exercise frequency [<i>F</i>(1,10) = 3.421, <i>p</i> = 0.094], intervention duration [<i>F</i>(1,10) = 0.0002, <i>p</i> = 0.988], and measurement tools [<i>F</i>(2,9) = 0.882, <i>p</i> = 0.447] all showed no significant moderating effects. Owing to the limited number of effect sizes in certain categories (<i>k</i> ≤ 2), interaction tests were not performed for exercise modality, and results across groups were presented descriptively. Descriptive analyses showed that the combinations of "aerobic + strength + balance + coordination + agility" training (<i>k</i> = 2, <i>g</i> = 2.109, 95% CI [0.816, 3.402], <i>p</i> = 0.006) and "aerobic + strength + flexibility" training (<i>k</i> = 2, <i>g</i> = 2.039, 95% CI [0.772, 3.307], <i>p</i> = 0.007) yielded large effect sizes. Interventions with session durations of 30-60 min improved global cognitive function (<i>g</i> = 1.236, 95% CI [0.151, 2.321], <i>p</i> = 0.030), as did those with frequencies of 4-5 sessions per week (<i>g</i> = 1.772, 95% CI [0.714, 2.830], <i>p</i> = 0.004). Assessments using both the MoCA (<i>g</i> = 1.337, 95% CI [0.235, 2.439], <i>p</i> = 0.023) and the MMSE (<i>g</i> = 1.054, 95% CI [0.214, 1.895], <i>p</i> = 0.020) supported the positive effects of multicomponent exercise on global cognition. With respect to executive function subdomains, cognitive flexibility was significantly improved (<i>g</i> = 0.437, 95% CI [0.112, 0.761], <i>p</i> = 0.014), whereas working memory and inhibitory control did not reach statistical significance.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="DISCUSSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">The overall methodological quality of the included studies was moderate; however, most studies did not implement allocation concealment or fully report blinding procedures, indicating a certain risk of bias. Tests for publication bias did not indicate significant bias. GRADE assessment showed that the quality of evidence was low for global cognitive function and moderate for executive function. Multicomponent exercise exerts positive effects on global cognitive function and executive function in older adults with MCI, whereas its effects on BDNF remain inconclusive. Future studies with more rigorous designs and adequate sample sizes are warranted to promote the personalized application of multicomponent exercise in the MCI population.</AbstractText><AbstractText
